claims.text: Mechanical alloying by high-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering can be used to prepare and mechanically evaluate HfNbTaTiZr alloys with varied compositions.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr material is equiatomic.
Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr powders can be produced by conventional mechanical alloying.
Systematically changing Hf content while holding milling, sintering, and testing conditions constant can isolate the effect of Hf percentage.
Room-temperature compression testing on cylindrical specimens is compatible with mechanically alloyed and spark-plasma-sintered refractory HEAs.
Changing Hf content can alter grain size, phase distribution, phase uniformity, and elemental segregation in HfNbTaTiZr.
Changing Hf content changes the extent of solid-solution strengthening in HfNbTaTiZr.
Changing Hf content influences grain growth during sintering.
Hf has a larger atomic radius than some of the other constituents of HfNbTaTiZr.
Increasing Hf content introduces additional lattice distortion.
The lattice distortion caused by additional Hf improves dislocation pinning.
Increasing Hf content enhances grain-boundary pinning and refines the microstructure.
A refined microstructure resists deformation more effectively and increases compressive strength.
Increasing Hf relative to the equiatomic baseline will produce finer grains and higher compressive strength.
Reducing Hf relative to the equiatomic baseline will produce coarser grains and lower compressive strength.
The predicted trend is expected to apply within approximately 10–20% relative deviation from the equiatomic Hf level under fixed processing conditions.
SEM, XRD, TEM, and elemental mapping can characterize the microstructure and phase distribution of mechanically alloyed and spark-plasma-sintered refractory HEAs.
Failure to observe both a statistically significant grain-size reduction and compressive-strength increase after increasing Hf would reject the hypothesis.
